intro: The sixth screen read the four redesigns as intended: the heavy seesaw, the dog begging and the lost balloon scored full marks in every picture ("the man's weight is holding his end down, so the girl is stuck up in the air while he reads"; "a blue balloon has got away"), and the person about to trip rose from 0.79 to 0.88. Inferences rose from 0.83 to 0.91, the best of six screens. But nine templates that passed in v0.8 slipped under the gate on their new pictures, most by a single half point, so 54 of 64 pass, down from 60. The largest is the dropped ice cream, whose empty cone cannot be told from a full one at picture size; the others have causes visible in the pictures (a fork sweeping on stepping stones read as digging, a floating box beside the house read as stuck in the wall).
screen: Inferences rose from 0.83 to 0.91: the set lost 3 inference points, half of them to the dropped ice cream. Contradictions fell from 1.00 to 0.95 on two half points (an upward stream reaching an awning read as dripping from it; a bucket on the head offered as "a tall blue hat"). Actions eased to 0.95 and unintended oddities rose to 2.3 per picture, among them an oversized sandwich and a stepping stone drawn over a dog. The one misread in the set was a sleeping cat, "crouched low".
redrawn: Three of the four redesigns pass with full marks. Every seesaw reader said the girl is stuck because of the man's weight or that he is ignoring her; every dog was "begging for the ice cream"; every balloon child had "just let go" of one balloon. The trip walker's big open book read as a book in all four pictures, but in the busiest garden she stood between the clothesline posts, where the book was "a book or papers" (or laundry to hang) and the bucket beside her drew no prediction.
gate: Every template was screened in at least two pictures. Eight of the ten failures are within one half point of the gate (one item read half-right, or one misread item read half-right, would pass them): with two pictures and two to six items, one reader's hedge decides it. The dropped ice cream (0.78 over five pictures) is the one clear legibility failure in the set: nobody could tell the cone is empty. The sweeping fork (on a garden's stepping stones, read as digging) and the floating box (beside the house corner, read as stuck in the wall) were each misread once in a probe.
